title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
hook: After a world war and the Holocaust, nations did something unprecedented: they wrote down, together, a common list of rights belonging to everyone on Earth.
key_points: The UDHR was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948, after World War II.
It sets out a common list of fundamental rights and freedoms for all people.
It is a declaration, not a binding treaty — but hugely influential as a global standard.
It inspired later binding treaties and many national constitutions and bills of rights.
content_html: In 1948, in the shadow of a world war and the Holocaust that had shown how completely a state could turn against its own people, the newly formed United Nations did something that had never been done before: its member nations agreed, together, on a written statement of the rights belonging to every human being on Earth. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), adopted by the General Assembly that year, was the result — a common standard listing fundamental rights and freedoms meant to apply to all people, everywhere.
extra_html: Its thirty articles range widely, from civil and political rights such as freedom from torture, equality before the law, and freedom of expression, to economic and social rights such as education, work, and an adequate standard of living. The United Nations describes the UDHR as a milestone document and the foundation of modern international human-rights law. A crucial point to understand is its legal status: the Declaration itself is not a binding treaty that states can be sued under — it is a statement of shared principles. Yet calling it "non-binding" badly undersells its influence. It established the common vocabulary and benchmark for human rights worldwide, and it directly inspired the binding international treaties that followed, as well as the rights provisions of countless national constitutions. The UDHR's enduring achievement was to make the universality of human rights an explicit, agreed-upon global standard rather than a philosopher's aspiration — setting the reference point against which governments could thereafter be measured and held to account.

related.title: What Human Rights Are
related.hook: Human rights are the radical claim that every person — regardless of country, status, or who's in charge — holds certain basic rights simply by being human.

related.title: Enforcing Human Rights
related.hook: Declaring a right is easy; enforcing it against a sovereign state is hard. The global human-rights system relies more on pressure and exposure than on a world police.

related.title: The UN & International Organizations
related.hook: Sovereign states that answer to no one above them still build standing clubs to cooperate. The UN is the largest — a forum, not a world government.
